title: DID GOD WRITE YOUR TRAGEDY… OR IS HE WEEPING WITH YOU IN THE MIDDLE OF IT?
paragraphs: DID GOD WRITE YOUR TRAGEDY… OR IS HE WEEPING WITH YOU IN THE MIDDLE OF IT?

When someone dies, a child suffers, or everything you prayed to protect falls apart, people say, “It was God's will.” But what if we've been blaming God for things His own heart does not delight in? The answer Jesus gave might change how you understand suffering, judgment, grace, and the God you thought you knew.
There is a sentence that has broken more wounded hearts than the people speaking it ever realized.
“God wanted it to happen.”
A mother stands beside a tiny coffin.
A husband watches the woman he promised to grow old with take her final breath.
A father loses the job that kept food on his family's table.
A young believer kneels beside a hospital bed, begging God for a miracle that never comes.
And somewhere in the silence, someone tries to comfort them.
“Everything happens for a reason.”
“God needed another angel.”
“This must be God's punishment.”
“It was His will.”
They mean well. Some genuinely believe they are defending God's sovereignty.
But imagine being that mother.
Imagine hearing that the God you trusted deliberately wanted your child dead.
Imagine being told that the Savior who welcomed little children into His arms somehow needed your baby more than you did.
And now imagine trying to pray to Him.
How do you run into the arms of Someone you've been taught to believe personally arranged the destruction of everything you loved?
Perhaps you've never said that question aloud.
Perhaps you've been afraid to.
Because somewhere along the way, you were taught that questioning what happened meant questioning God Himself.
But there is a difference between questioning God's goodness and desperately trying to understand it.
And Scripture gives us something far more profound than the easy answers people offer at funerals.
God is sovereign over suffering. But that does not mean He delights in suffering.
Those two truths belong together.
And if we separate them, we can turn the Father revealed by Jesus Christ into someone Scripture never intended us to imagine.
Listen carefully to the words of Lamentations.
“For though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men.” — Lamentations 3:32–33, KJV
Read that again.
Not quickly.
Read it like someone who has spent years wondering whether God enjoyed watching their life collapse.
“He doth not afflict willingly.”
The Hebrew is extraordinarily important here.
Lamentations 3:33 contains the expression:
כִּי לֹא עִנָּה מִלִּבּוֹ
Ki lo ʿinnah millibbo.
Literally, the phrase communicates that He does not afflict “from His heart.”
The Hebrew word לִבּוֹ (libbo) means “his heart,” and מִלִּבּוֹ (millibbo) means “from his heart.”
In biblical Hebrew, the heart represents the inner person, including the will, thoughts, and desires.
The verse is not saying God has no purpose when He permits or brings affliction.
It is saying something more tender.
Affliction is not something God takes pleasure in for its own sake.
He is not a cruel spectator entertained by human tears.
He is not a sadistic ruler looking for someone to hurt.
He is not indifferent to the suffering of His creatures.
And yet, we must not remove these words from their setting.
Lamentations was written against the terrible backdrop of Jerusalem's destruction. God's people had experienced devastation connected to covenant unfaithfulness and divine judgment.
The same passage that says God does not afflict from His heart also says, “Though he cause grief.”
That matters.
The Bible does not teach that God merely watches history unfold without authority or involvement.

Sometimes Scripture explicitly describes suffering as divine judgment. Sometimes it describes suffering as discipline. Sometimes suffering results from human wickedness, life in a fallen world, or circumstances whose purposes remain hidden from us.
But the Bible does not give us permission to declare that every tragedy is God's punishment for a particular sin.
And Jesus confronted precisely that dangerous assumption.
There was a day when people approached Him with news of a horrifying incident.
Some Galileans had been killed by Pontius Pilate, and their blood had been mingled with their sacrifices.
Think about the horror.
These were people involved in worship.
They had come into a religious setting, and violence had found them there.
Imagine the families waiting for them to return.
Imagine the confusion.
The unanswered questions.
The terror of discovering that people who had gone to offer sacrifices would never come home.
And beneath the report was a question humanity still asks whenever tragedy strikes.
What did they do to deserve this?
Jesus answered:
“Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.” — Luke 13:2–3, KJV
Then Jesus brought up another tragedy.
A tower in Siloam had collapsed, killing eighteen people.
No murderer is identified in that incident.
No specific moral failure is assigned to the victims.
A structure fell.
Eighteen lives ended.
And Jesus asked whether those who died were worse offenders than everyone else living in Jerusalem.
Again, His answer was no.
Do you understand what Jesus was dismantling?
The assumption that the people who suffer most must be the people who have sinned most.
He refused to let the living turn the dead into convenient examples of divine punishment.
He refused to let tragedy become evidence that its victims were spiritually inferior.
And He redirected His listeners toward something they desperately needed to hear.
The question is not whether those people were worse sinners than you. The question is whether you are ready to meet God yourself.
In Luke 13:3 and 13:5, the Greek word translated “repent” is:
μετανοῆτε — metanoēte.
It comes from the verb μετανοέω (metanoeō), meaning to repent, to undergo a change of mind and direction.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling guilty.
It is a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in the way we live.
Jesus was not saying, “Repent, or I will make a tower fall on you.”
He was warning that physical death exposes the urgency of a deeper spiritual reality.
Life is fragile.
Judgment is real.
And no one should confuse another person's tragedy with proof of their own righteousness.
The Galileans were not uniquely wicked because Pilate killed them.
The eighteen were not uniquely guilty because the tower collapsed.
And the person reading these words is not automatically under special divine punishment because something terrible happened to them.
That distinction could rescue someone's faith.
Perhaps yours.
Because some people are not running away from God because they love their sin.
Some are struggling to approach Him because they have been taught to see His anger behind every ambulance, every diagnosis, every miscarriage, every accident, and every grave.
They have confused God's sovereign authority with the idea that He must personally delight in every painful event.
But Scripture is more careful than that.
The Bible teaches that God rules over creation and history. Nothing takes Him by surprise. Nothing exists outside His ultimate authority.
Yet God's sovereignty does not make Him morally responsible for evil in the same way that sinful human beings are responsible for the evil they choose.
James 1:13 declares that God does not tempt anyone with evil.
Deuteronomy 32:4 describes His ways as just.
Psalm 145:17 says the Lord is righteous in all His ways.
And Ezekiel 33:11 reveals that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but calls them to turn and live.
God's holiness is not suspended when suffering occurs.
Neither is His compassion.
We must be careful with the word allow, too.
It can be helpful when distinguishing God's permission from His moral approval. But it must not suggest that God is powerless, surprised, or absent.

Scripture sometimes describes God actively bringing judgment. At other times, it describes Him permitting sinful actions without approving their evil. And in many individual tragedies, Scripture does not reveal why God allowed what happened.
We should never pretend to know what He has not told us.
There are mysteries that cannot be solved by a slogan.
And sometimes the most faithful thing a Christian can say beside a hospital bed is not, “I know exactly why God did this.”
Sometimes it is simply:
“I don't know why this happened. But I know Jesus has not abandoned you. And I'm staying here with you.”
That is not weak theology.
That is love refusing to manufacture certainty.
Consider Job.
A man loses his possessions.
His children die.
His health collapses.
And his friends arrive with explanations.
Surely he must have done something wrong.
Surely suffering this severe must indicate hidden sin.
Surely God would not permit such devastation without Job deserving it.
But the reader knows something Job's friends do not.
Their accusation is false.
Job's suffering cannot be explained by the simple equation they keep defending.
And at the end of the book, God rebukes those friends for failing to speak rightly about Him.
How many wounded believers have encountered modern versions of Job's friends?
People who examine someone's tragedy like detectives searching for a secret sin.
People who turn grief into an interrogation.
People who insist that if your faith were stronger, your child would have survived, your marriage would have remained intact, or your body would have been healed.
That is not the message of Job.
And it is not the message of Jesus in Luke 13.
Sometimes people suffer because others commit evil.
Sometimes people suffer because creation itself is broken.
Sometimes God disciplines His children for their good, as Hebrews 12 teaches.
Sometimes Scripture identifies a particular judgment.
But we cannot assign a divine explanation to every individual tragedy simply because we believe God is sovereign.
There is a reason Romans 8:22 describes creation as groaning.
The world is not yet what it will be.
Death is still an enemy.
Sin has wounded human history.
And even believers who belong to Christ continue to experience sorrow while awaiting the final redemption of their bodies.
Christian faith does not require pretending that everything painful is good.
It requires trusting that God can remain good even when what happens is genuinely terrible.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Because Jesus did not come into a world of suffering and merely explain it from a safe distance.
He entered it.
He was born into human vulnerability.
He knew hunger.
He knew exhaustion.
He knew betrayal.
He knew what it meant to be misunderstood by people closest to Him.
He stood before a tomb where someone He loved had died.
And in John 11:35, Scripture gives us two words:
“Jesus wept.”
The Greek is:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς — edakrysen ho Iēsous.
“Jesus wept.”
The verb ἐδάκρυσεν refers to shedding tears.
And here is what makes that moment so astonishing.
Jesus knew He was about to raise Lazarus.
He knew the grave would not have the final word that day.
He knew His own authority over death.
And still He wept.
Knowing the outcome did not make Him indifferent to the pain.
His power did not erase His compassion.
His knowledge did not silence His tears.
So why do we sometimes speak as though trusting God means never grieving?
Why do we tell broken people to stop crying when the Son of God Himself cried?
Jesus did not stand outside Lazarus's tomb and rebuke Mary and Martha for having emotions.
He entered their sorrow.
He listened.
He spoke.
He wept.
And then He called Lazarus out of the grave.
This is the Savior Christians are invited to trust.
Not a distant deity amused by human misery.
Not a powerless observer unable to intervene.
But the incarnate Son of God, full of truth, compassion, and authority.
Yet even the raising of Lazarus was not the final answer to human suffering.
Lazarus would eventually face physical death again.
A greater victory was coming.
And it would come through something the world could only describe as a scandal.
The cross.
Think about it.
An innocent Man was betrayed.
False witnesses testified against Him.
Religious leaders demanded His death.
A Roman governor authorized His execution.
Soldiers mocked and tortured Him.
And the only perfectly righteous human being who ever lived was nailed to wood.
If anyone had looked at that scene without knowing the resurrection was coming, they might have asked:
“Where is God?”
“Why would He allow this?”
“How could anything good possibly come from something so evil?”
And yet Scripture tells us that this darkest moment became the place where God's saving purpose was accomplished.
Acts 2:23 says Jesus was delivered up according to God's determined counsel and foreknowledge, while also holding those who crucified Him responsible for their lawless actions.
Do not miss the distinction.
God's redemptive purpose did not make the betrayal righteous.
It did not make the false accusations truthful.
It did not make the cruelty holy.
Human beings committed real evil.
And God accomplished salvation through what they meant for destruction.
The cross does not teach us that evil becomes good because God can redeem it.
It teaches us that evil cannot ultimately defeat God's good purpose.
That is a breathtaking difference.
And it changes how we speak about tragedy.
We do not have to call a child's death beautiful.
We do not have to describe abuse as a blessing.
We do not have to tell someone that their suffering was secretly wonderful.
We can name evil as evil.
We can mourn death as death.
We can condemn injustice as injustice.
And still believe that the risen Christ is powerful enough to bring redemption into places human beings thought were beyond repair.
Romans 8:28 says that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
It does not say all things are good.
And the next verse, Romans 8:29, connects God's purpose to conforming His people to the image of His Son.
The promise is not that every painful experience will produce an immediate earthly reward.
It is not that every disease will disappear.
It is not that every broken relationship will be restored.
It is not that every grieving parent will understand why their child died.
It is that God's saving purpose in Christ cannot finally be overthrown by suffering.
And that promise rests on something stronger than our ability to explain what happened.
It rests on the crucified and risen Jesus.
Perhaps you have been carrying a question for years.
Why did God let my father die?
Why did my child have to suffer?
Why did the person I trusted betray me?
Why did I pray so desperately and still lose what I loved?
Why did God seem silent when I needed Him most?
I will not insult your pain by pretending I know the answer to your particular tragedy.
I don't.
And anyone who confidently claims to know God's secret purpose in every loss should remember the humility Scripture requires.
But I can tell you what the Gospel reveals.
God has not left the world without hope.
Christ has entered our suffering.
He has borne our sins.
He has conquered the grave.
And He promises a future in which death itself will be destroyed.
Revelation 21:4 does not promise that believers will never cry in this present age.
It promises a coming day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
Notice the tenderness.
He does not merely announce that sorrow is finished.
He wipes away tears.
The final Christian hope is not that we will eventually learn to call every tragedy good.
It is that God will make all things new.
And until that day, we are allowed to lament.
We are allowed to ask why.
We are allowed to kneel with trembling hands and pray through tears.
We are allowed to say, as the psalmists did, “How long, O LORD?”
Faith is not always a confident voice declaring victory.
Sometimes faith is a broken whisper that says:
“Jesus, I don't understand. But I still need You.”
And perhaps that is where you are right now.
Not rebellious.
Not pretending.
Just exhausted.
You have heard so many explanations that you no longer know what to believe.
You have smiled through church services while quietly wondering whether God is angry with you.
You have watched other people celebrate answered prayers while you continue visiting a grave.
And the hardest part is not merely what happened.
It is the fear that God Himself might have become your enemy.
Hear the invitation of Christ.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus calls the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest.
He does not demand that they solve the mystery of suffering before approaching Him.
He calls them to Himself.
And the same Jesus who invites the weary also calls sinners to repentance.
Because the Gospel is not merely comfort for wounded emotions.
It is salvation for people separated from God by sin.
We all need forgiveness.
We all need grace.
We all need the righteousness that we cannot produce for ourselves.
Jesus died for our sins and rose again, as 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 declares.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
You do not need to deny your grief to repent.
You do not need to understand every tragedy to trust Christ.
You do not need to pretend you are healed before coming to the One who saves.
Come honestly.
Bring your sin.
Bring your anger.
Bring your questions.
Bring the memories that still hurt.
Bring the prayers you are afraid to pray.
And remember that the God who calls you to surrender is the God who gave His Son for sinners.
The cross is not proof that God delights in suffering. It is the supreme revelation of how far His love went to redeem sinners through suffering.
That is why our message has always been:
Not because Jesus erases history.
Not because He makes every earthly consequence disappear.
Not because He promises that Christians will never suffer again.
But because shame does not have to be your final identity.
Sin does not have to remain your master.
Your past does not have to determine your eternal future.
And death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
The scandal of the cross became the proclamation of grace.
The condemned Savior rose as the victorious Lord.
And people who once stood guilty before God can now receive forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
That is a story worth telling.
Not because it makes us famous.
Not because it guarantees a comfortable life.
But because there are still people who have never heard the Gospel clearly.
There are people sitting in church pews who believe God hates them.
There are grieving families who have mistaken careless religious statements for the voice of Christ.
There are believers silently losing hope because nobody has helped them distinguish biblical truth from assumptions about suffering.
And there are people scrolling through Facebook right now who may be carrying the very questions you once carried.
That is why I want to ask you for something meaningful.
Not simply to increase its reach.
Someone may be afraid to return to church.
Someone may be angry with God.
Someone may need to discover that Jesus is not repelled by their tears.
You do not need to expose anyone's private pain publicly to help them.
Sometimes the most compassionate thing we can do is place biblical hope within reach of someone who is too exhausted to search for it.
Have you ever struggled to understand why God allowed something painful in your life?
You do not have to share details you want to keep private.
Let this be a place where people can be honest without being condemned for grieving.
Where testimonies can strengthen the weary.
Where Scripture can correct misunderstandings.
Where those who are hurting can be reminded that they are not walking alone.
Not because you must return to these words every day, but because there may come a night when grief speaks louder than your memory of God's promises.
On that night, return to Lamentations 3.
Return to Luke 13.
Return to John 11.
Return to the cross.
And remember what Scripture actually says.
Our desire is to help people move beyond shallow religious slogans into a deeper understanding of Scripture, repentance, grace, and daily discipleship.
And for those who feel called to help this ministry continue and expand, I want to extend a personal invitation.
It does not purchase forgiveness.
It does not make your prayers more powerful.
And it is not a biblical requirement for proving your love for Jesus.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Christ, not something earned through financial support.
But Scripture does encourage believers to support faithful Gospel work with willing and generous hearts.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–17 shows how believers can participate in Gospel ministry through material support.
Your local congregation, its shepherding, worship, fellowship, and mission remain deeply important.
A way of saying, “I want this message of Jesus Christ to reach more people.”
We want people to have access to resources that encourage careful Bible study, spiritual maturity, repentance, prayer, and a stronger relationship with Christ.
These are simply tangible expressions of thanks. They are not the reason to give, and they are never a measure of anyone's spiritual worth.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
Helping more people open their Bibles.
Helping more people understand the Gospel.
Helping more people discover that their deepest hope is not found in an explanation for every tragedy, but in Jesus Christ Himself.
You are welcome here.
Keep reading Scripture.
Keep praying.
Keep growing.
Keep sharing the truth.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Before you leave, I want you to remember the question that brought us here.
Does God cause every tragedy, or does He sometimes allow what He does not delight in?
Scripture does not give us a simplistic answer that treats every painful event in exactly the same way.
It reveals a sovereign God who can judge, discipline, permit, restrain, and redeem according to His perfect wisdom.
It reveals a God who does not delight in affliction for its own sake.
It reveals a Savior who refuses to equate every victim's suffering with exceptional personal sin.
It reveals Jesus weeping at a grave.
And it reveals the Son of God rising from His own grave, guaranteeing that death itself will one day be defeated.
So when the next tragedy comes, be careful what you say to the grieving.
Do not rush to explain God's hidden purposes.
Do not accuse the wounded.
Do not turn a funeral into a courtroom.
Do not call evil good.
Sit beside them.
Weep with them.
Pray with them.
Help them carry what feels unbearable.
And when the moment is right, gently point them toward Jesus.
Because the greatest comfort Christianity offers is not a complete explanation of why every terrible thing happens.
It is the revelation of a crucified and risen Savior who will not abandon His people and who will one day make all things new.
And perhaps tonight, when you finally close your eyes, you will still have questions.
You may still miss someone.
You may still wish the story had unfolded differently.
You may still have tears.
But you can bring those tears to Christ.
You can trust His revealed character without pretending to understand His every purpose.
And you can hold on to the promise that the grave is not the end of the story for those who belong to Him.
The tragedy may have broken your heart, but it has not broken the promise of the Savior who will one day wipe away your tears.
